title: Seeing health and social care work through the lens of ‘connective professionalism’: Implications for interprofessional education
text_snippet: Seeing health and social care work through the lens of ‘connective professionalism’: Implications for interprofessional education Abstract Background: The field of interprofessional education provides educational preparedness for collaborative work. In this cross‐cutting edge paper, we argue that aligning educational offerings to diverse current and future configurations of collaborative work is both a goal and a challenge for educators. To continue to move towards this goal, we draw from recent debates in the fields of organizational studies and sociology of professions. In response to the historical focus on protective professionalism, theorists in the intersections of those two fields have begun to debate the concept of ‘connective professionalism’. Analytical contribution: Connective professionalism offers a lens to view the diversity of collaborative work that occurs across the health and social care system. It challenges a static notion of professionalism, roles and boundaries and instead treats professional work as a continually negotiated accomplishment. This lively theoretical debate is happening outside of health professions education journals but is particularly relevant for the domain of interprofessional education. title: Becoming a physician–scientist: Early research participation as an identity sandbox for preclinical medical students
text_snippet: Becoming a physician–scientist: Early research participation as an identity sandbox for preclinical medical students Abstract Introduction Early participation in research is a widely used strategy to encourage medical students to pursue physician–scientist careers. Yet its influence on professional identity formation (PIF) remains poorly understood. We explored how participation in an extracurricular research programme during preclinical education influenced students' emerging professional identities, aiming to inform programmes that support students' PIF as physician–scientists alongside research skill development. Method We conducted a cross‐sectional qualitative study at a Dutch medical school offering an extracurricular research programme for preclinical medical students. Twelve medical students created a Rich Picture depicting a memorable programme experience that influenced their personal and professional development and were subsequently interviewed. Rich Pictures and interview transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with Communities of Practice concepts incorporated iteratively to deepen interpretation. title: Validity in competency‐based health professions education
text_snippet: Validity in competency‐based health professions education Abstract Introduction Validity is a term that carries significant weight within health professions education (HPE), particularly with regard to learner assessment. Validity theory has changed significantly over the last century, transforming in concert with education, measurement and assessment practices. Most recently, HPE has adopted the conceptualisation of validity as an argument supporting the interpretation (and sometimes uses) of assessment data. The spread of competency‐based education and programmatic assessment has introduced new tensions and opportunities for operationalising argument‐based approaches to validity. Methods The authors used a selective interpretive synthesis of the literature to explore how current argument‐based validity frameworks can be extended to support the complexity of programmatic assessment and to meet the social imperative of public protection that is core to competency‐based education. title: Scripted success, unscripted consequences: How assessments in undergraduate medical education shape physician identity formation
text_snippet: Scripted success, unscripted consequences: How assessments in undergraduate medical education shape physician identity formation Abstract Introduction Professional identity formation (PIF) is increasingly understood not only as becoming a physician but as a matter of being and belonging within the profession. The development of a holistic professional identity can enhance a physician's confidence, wellbeing and performance. Assessment is a central site of the socialisation through which PIF occurs, yet how learners experience assessment when it is felt to be biassed or exclusionary, and what this means for their identity formation, is not well understood. We aimed to explore if and how medical students experience identity‐related challenges, including microaggressions, through assessment and how these experiences shape their developing professional identities. Methods We conducted a constructivist qualitative study using semi‐structured interviews, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Medical students at a single Canadian institution who self‐identified in response to an emailed invitation as having had uncomfortable, unsettling or identity‐related experiences with assessment were interviewed. title: Brittle threshold: When adaptive success is the warning sign
text_snippet: Brittle threshold: When adaptive success is the warning sign Abstract Context What happens when a system keeps working—not because it is well designed but because people keep absorbing the strain? That question stayed with me after studying a community‐led vaccination clinic during the COVID‐19 pandemic. It delivered hundreds of vaccinations a day, with no formal chain of command or protocols. By any measure, it was a success. What it cost to sustain that success was never examined. Across my empirical work, I kept encountering the same pattern: systems functioning because people stretched roles, coordinated through workarounds and relied on relationships that were not designed to carry the full load. These adaptations were effective. Yet they were also hiding strain. Conceptual Contribution In this paper, I introduce Brittle Threshold as a concept for attending to this condition. Rather than treating adaptive action as evidence of success, Brittle Threshold frames adaptive action as diagnostic information: evidence of how a system is coping and how close it may be operating to its limits. title: 73 days?! Examining the rate at which medical knowledge doubles and its implications
text_snippet: 73 days?! Examining the rate at which medical knowledge doubles and its implications Abstract The Issue: ‘Knowledge is accumulating faster than human‐beings have the capacity to assimilate it’. According to popular estimate, knowledge now doubles every 73 days, roughly the lifespan of a housefly. We need, therefore, to stop thinking of health professional education in terms of transmission of knowledge. Instead, we need to focus training programmes on enabling learners to use the increasingly powerful technologies that are revolutionizing how health care is practiced. And we need to stop using assessments that seem increasingly inauthentic by virtue of precluding learners from using such technologies. Reflections: Do we? Do we really? This Medical Education Mythology paper explores the origin of the prominent claim that medical knowledge doubles every 73 days, offers an empirical assessment of its veracity and outlines several repercussions that can arise if we accept the estimate without critical appraisal. In doing so, we encourage reflection on the implications of the exponential rate at which knowledge is increasing at the same time as urging caution against panic‐driven education practices. title: Looking beyond the individual: Conceptualizing assessment validity as interdependence within teams
text_snippet: Looking beyond the individual: Conceptualizing assessment validity as interdependence within teams Abstract Validity Over the last century, validity theory has evolved from Kelley's foundational work on educational measurement through Cronbach and Meehl's construct validation, to Messick's unified framework and, finally, Kane's argument‐based approach. Throughout this evolution, one premise remained neglected: The unit of analysis is the individual. Focusing primarily on the individual is problematic, especially in Medicine where constructs like clinical competence are treated as a possession of an individual, and contextual factors such as team configurations are considered statistical nuisances. The clinical landscape has also evolved: Modern patient care is delivered by large, interprofessional teams whose collective competence provides care that no single individual could alone. The disconnect between the primacy of independent performance and the interdependent nature of healthcare delivery poses a validity threat to assessment systems that routinely attribute performance to an individual but fail to account for interdependence, teams and context. title: ‘Tell me what you know’: Written recall as a window into illness script quality
text_snippet: ‘Tell me what you know’: Written recall as a window into illness script quality Abstract Introduction Illness scripts (mental representations of disease knowledge) are central to diagnostic expertise, yet structured methods to examine their quality across medical training are lacking. This exploratory study investigated whether textual indicators derived from free‐recall protocols could reveal aspects of illness script quality in medical students. Methods In this cross‐sectional study, students from years one through six at seven Brazilian medical schools completed a free‐recall task for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and myocardial infarction (MI) after a progress test. Written responses were segmented into idea units (IUs) and analysed for accuracy (correct idea units), scope (number of disease dimensions), organisation (balanced adjusted ratio of clustering) and encapsulation (higher‐order summary terms). Differences across training years were examined using Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn tests. title: Patient and public engagement in the CanMEDS framework: Which patients? Which publics?
text_snippet: Patient and public engagement in the CanMEDS framework: Which patients? Which publics? Abstract Introduction Medical education institutions increasingly employ patient and public engagement (PPE) to inform their learning activities. While this shift is highly welcome, it is equally important to consider whether and how patient and public perspectives have been incorporated in globally influential texts, such as the CanMEDS 2015 Physician Competency Framework, that govern the contexts in which these activities play out, particularly as this framework undergoes revision. Methods We explored PPE in the creation and revision of CanMEDS, applying textual analysis to an archive that included the current framework, its drafts and revision documents, earlier iterations (e.g. CanMEDS 2005 and 2000) and ancillary texts. We specifically examined patient and public involvement on committees, in expert working groups and in consultation processes. Results Findings indicate that despite stated desires to include ‘the perspectives of the people who depend on Canadian physicians for their health care’, there was minimal PPE in the 3‐year revision process that led to CanMEDS 2015. title: Myths we tell ourselves about validity: A justice‐oriented reckoning in medical education
text_snippet: Myths we tell ourselves about validity: A justice‐oriented reckoning in medical education Abstract Background Medical education has moved beyond debating whether objectivity in assessment is achievable, acknowledging that assessment is inherently subjective. Yet the pursuit of objectivity, through standardisation, bias reduction and statistical rigour, remains a cherished goal. This paper argues that this lingering pursuit of objectivity undermines strong validity arguments and produces assessments that fail to engage meaningfully with the lived realities and possible futures of marginalised learners and patients. Theoretical Framework Drawing on justice‐oriented assessment validity (JAV) frameworks and disability critical race theory (DisCrit), we examine four pervasive myths in medical education assessment: (1) Constructs are universal and stable, (2) removing bias from assessment is sufficient, (3) flexibility decreases rigour and (4) numbers are neutral. These myths allow educators to make validity arguments that ignore or explain away harm. We demonstrate how each myth, when examined from the standpoint of disabled, racially and ethnically marginalised learners, reveals itself as both inaccurate and harmful. title: Validity considerations in programmatic assessment of clinical reasoning
text_snippet: Validity considerations in programmatic assessment of clinical reasoning Abstract Problem Clinical reasoning is a core competency in health professions education, but its assessment is challenging. Clinical reasoning is multifaceted, content‐ and context‐dependent, and largely unobservable, and no single assessment can support a robust characterisation of a learner's clinical reasoning. Programmatic assessment has gained traction as a response to these challenges, but a validity argument explaining why a programmatic approach addresses the specific vulnerabilities of clinical reasoning assessment has received limited attention. Approach We examine validity issues in the programmatic assessment of clinical reasoning using Kane's argument‐based framework, organised around five inferences: performance, scoring, generalisation, extrapolation and consequences. For each inference, we identify the central validity question, describe issues specific to clinical reasoning at the level of the individual assessment and the programme, discuss how a programmatic approach mitigates weaknesses of single assessments and describe residual or new validity threats. title: Assessment fairness at the nexus of validity: Linking fairness threats to score meaning
text_snippet: Assessment fairness at the nexus of validity: Linking fairness threats to score meaning Abstract Introduction Nearly a century after Kelley's seminal work Interpretation of educational measurements , we revisit the concept of validity to argue that fairness is not a downstream equity add‐on but a core requirement throughout the assessment lifecycle. In health professions education, where assessment decisions shape learner progression and patient care, validity arguments must justify the meaning and use of scores for all examinees in equity‐relevant contexts. Methods We advance a fairness‐as‐validity position: Fairness consists of validity claims about whether scores carry comparable meaning and support defensible decisions across groups. In this framing, fairness threats are validity threats when construct underrepresentation or construct‐irrelevant variance systematically alters what scores represent. We distinguish these threats from test misuse and situate fairness evaluation within argument‐based validation and the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing. title: Now you see me, now you don't: A critical narrative review of educator identity in health professions education
text_snippet: Now you see me, now you don't: A critical narrative review of educator identity in health professions education Abstract Introduction Health professions educators occupy a unique position at the intersection of clinical practice, education and service. Despite their central role, educator identity remains under‐recognised and insufficiently theorised within academic medicine, where clinical expertise and research dominate traditional hierarchies of value. This review offers an integrated understanding of educator identity by foregrounding the interplay among the self, institutional structures and the broader sociocultural milieu of health professions education (HPE). Methods We conducted a critical narrative review using an interpretive approach. A multidisciplinary Scopus search identified empirical and non‐empirical English‐language studies published between 2000 and 2025 that engaged conceptually with educator identity in HPE. Selected studies were analysed through a layered interpretive lens drawing on sociological, psychological, psychosocial and sociocultural perspectives to examine how educator identity is conceptualised, negotiated and sustained within sociocultural context of the field. title: Developing validity arguments for artificial intelligence‐based assessment: Balancing affordances and threats
text_snippet: Developing validity arguments for artificial intelligence‐based assessment: Balancing affordances and threats Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to generate, score and interpret educational assessment, yet these applications are being adopted in a largely unregulated environment. This creates a paradox: Whereas AI systems used in clinical care are subject to formal scrutiny for safety, performance and monitoring, AI systems used to inform consequential decisions about learner progression and future clinical practice are not. Existing validity frameworks remain useful but may not fully account for AI‐specific threats. Methods We conducted a state‐of‐the‐science conceptual review examining validity for AI‐based assessment through Kane's four inferences: scoring, generalisation, extrapolation and implications. We integrated conceptual and empirical literature from medical education and adjacent AI evaluation fields to identify major threats, evidence needs and practical implications for defensible AI‐based assessment use. title: Unravelling student engagement orientations within peer assessment in team‐based learning: A constructivist grounded theory study
text_snippet: Unravelling student engagement orientations within peer assessment in team‐based learning: A constructivist grounded theory study Abstract Introduction While peer assessment in Team‐Based Learning is intended to foster students' academic skills and core competencies, implementation often falls short of meeting these goals. Because students' engagement is shaped by their beliefs and motivation, this research explored how they perceive and engage with peer assessment. Methods We conducted a constructivist grounded theory study at a Brazilian medical school with a 6‐year curriculum centred on collaborative Team‐Based Learning in rotating teams. Fifteen students were purposefully sampled and interviewed. Data were analysed inductively in an iterative way, using focused coding and constant comparison. Results Students differed in how they valued, provided and responded to peer assessment and in how peer assessment was influenced by contextual factors. We identified three distinct engagement orientations: requirement‐, team‐ and peer‐oriented. Requirement‐oriented students treated peer assessment as a formal obligation and offered generic feedback. Team‐oriented students focused on improving team functioning. Peer‐oriented students engaged deeply with peer assessment as a tool for both team and personal development

title: ‘I've been here before, but never looked at the ceiling’: Narratives of medical trainees who took illness‐based leaves
text_snippet: ‘I've been here before, but never looked at the ceiling’: Narratives of medical trainees who took illness‐based leaves Abstract Introduction Medical training is commonly imagined as a linear, uninterrupted progression, yet many trainees experience illness that necessitates a leave of absence (LOA). Illness‐based leaves may be especially fraught given stigma, opaque processes and training cultures that prioritise endurance. Little is known about how trainees experience illness and illness‐based leaves. Methods We conducted a narrative inquiry using Riessman's narrative analysis framework. Canadian physicians who had taken an illness‐based LOA during medical school or residency were recruited nationwide. Semi‐structured, in‐depth interviews were completed between December 2022 and July 2023, audio‐recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Analysis was inductive and iterative, examining narrative content and structure to understand participants' meaning‐making and shifting positioning within their stories. Rigour was supported through reflexive practice, collaborative team analysis and Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ)‐informed reporting. title: Error replication as an instructional strategy in simulation‐based procedural learning
text_snippet: Error replication as an instructional strategy in simulation‐based procedural learning Abstract Background Errors are an inevitable part of clinical learning, yet procedural training commonly emphasises error avoidance. This study examined the effect of deliberate replication of predefined procedural errors (Error Replication; ER), compared with error avoidance training (EAT), on post‐test performance, retention and transfer in surgical simulation. Methods In this randomised controlled trial, 70 medical students with no prior simulation‐based osteosynthesis experience completed a pre‐test of simulated dynamic hip screw (DHS) fixation before 60 min of ER or EAT training. ER participants deliberately reproduced predefined, clinically relevant errors, whereas EAT participants used simulator feedback to improve performance and minimise errors across successive iterations. Participants then completed an immediate DHS post‐test, a DHS retention test after 6–10 days and a transfer test involving antegrade femoral nailing. Transfer‐test performance was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included performance trajectories across pre‐test, post‐test and retention test; completed DHS iterations; self‐perceived dexterity and spatial awareness; and perceived training efficacy

title: The impact of role conflict on retention intentions of trainees participating in standardised residency training: A moderated mediation model
text_snippet: The impact of role conflict on retention intentions of trainees participating in standardised residency training: A moderated mediation model Abstract Introduction The standardised residency training stage involves high work demands and multiple role pressures, which may threaten the retention of residency trainees. Based on Conservation of Resources theory, either the mediating processes (resource depletion) or the moderating processes (resource compensation) may explain how role‐related sources of stress influence the retention intention of residency trainees, although how these processes operate within the structural design of residency training has not been well explored. Methods In a cross‐sectional survey, 350 residents in standardised residency training at People's Hospital in China were included (response rate 94.1%). Role conflict, burnout, salary satisfaction and retention intention were surveyed. PROCESS Models 4 and 15 with bootstrap confidence intervals were used to examine the mediation and moderation effects. title: Caring through uncertainty: Health professionals' perspectives on contributing to medical students' workplace learning
text_snippet: Caring through uncertainty: Health professionals' perspectives on contributing to medical students' workplace learning Abstract Purpose There is valuable learning embedded in interprofessional interactions that helps shape how medical students become physicians on health‐care teams. However, little is known about the perspectives of these other health professionals (OHPs) on when and how they impact medical students' workplace learning. This study explores how OHPs approach interacting with medical students and how they view their contributions to students' workplace learning. Method Using constructivist grounded theory methodology, researchers conducted 20 semi‐structured interviews with nurses, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, physician assistants, and social workers at four hospital systems affiliated with one medical school. Interview data were iteratively collected and analysed between June and December 2025 to generate a conceptual understanding of OHPs' perspectives on how their workplace interactions with medical students contribute to students' learning. title: Understanding how disability and ethnicity impact UK undergraduate and postgraduate medical training: A critical review
text_snippet: Understanding how disability and ethnicity impact UK undergraduate and postgraduate medical training: A critical review Abstract Introduction In recent years, the challenges associated with having a disability and being from a minority ethnic background have emerged from the literature in terms of medical training, career choice and progression, but how these characteristics intersect is less known. Understanding this intersection may improve support mechanisms, promote diversity and enhance workforce retention. This critical review aimed to evaluate all published empirical evidence regarding the impact of disability and ethnicity on the training of UK medical students and qualified doctors, with a specific focus on their intersection. Methods The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed. A range of medical‐, nursing‐ and psychology‐based bibliographic databases were used with no date restrictions. Quality appraisal was undertaken for all studies using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). A textual narrative method was used to synthesise the data.
